Try a 30-second question

£100 rises 20%, then falls 20%. How much remains?

100+20%
120−20%
?

Original hypothetical example. £ denotes pounds sterling.

You can start thinking quantitatively before you can code.

For the curious beginner

Want to understand returns, risk and backtests without memorising formulas in isolation? Bring basic arithmetic, percentages, paper and a calculator. No finance or Python background is assumed for the core route.

What will you have to show for it?

01

Calculations you can trace

Work through returns, compounding, present value, volatility, drawdown and portfolio weights. Keep a hand check and state the conventions.

02

Comparisons you can defend

Inspect data quality, signal and execution timing, costs and benchmarks. Retain unfavourable evidence instead of selecting the prettiest backtest.

03

A research memo you can explain

Connect a question to evidence, limitations and a specific revision. “Insufficient evidence” is a valid conclusion; profit is not a passing criterion.

A sequence that builds on itself

01–04

Build the foundations

Markets, financial mathematics, careful data handling, probability and statistics.

05–07

Understand risk and portfolios

Performance measures, diversification, simulation and derivative payoffs.

08–10

Develop a research process

Transparent backtests, research reliability, traceable evidence and a capstone memo.

Know what you are starting

Original hypothetical data support formative self-study. Study times and learning effectiveness have not been validated with learners. Self-checks do not establish independently graded competence or award a credential. No personal investment advice is provided.

No personal financial data is needed. The course has no answer uploads or analytics. Progress stays in this browser, separately by language; exports are records, not sync or restore. Optional Python downloads its runtime from jsDelivr on first use.

This hosted edition retains the site’s existing access permissions. A sign-in requirement is not an enrolment or payment flow.
